newsitem.title: USA: Revco says Big B is good fit.
newsitem.headline: Revco says Big B is good fit.

text.p: Revco D.S. Inc's $15-a-share tender offer for the 397-store Big B Inc reflects a good geographic fit between the two drugstore chains and is unlikely to run into antitrust roadblocks, Revco and analysts said Monday.
Earlier this year, government antitrust concerns derailed the largest U.S. drug chain, Rite Aid Corp, in its $1.8 billion bid to acquire Revco, the second largest.
"Revco and Big B are a natural fit," Revco President and Chief Executive Officer D. Dwayne Hoven said in a conference call.
"Geographically, Revco and Big B represent an excellent fit with only limited overlap of stores and distribution centers," he said.
Hoven said Revco was sensitive to U.S. Federal Trade Commission antitrust concerns and was "comfortable that we will gain FTC approval for this."

Big B, based in Alabama, operates mainly in that state and Georgia, with some stores in Florida, Tennessee and Mississippi. Revco, based in Twinsburg, Ohio, has 2,184 stores in 14 Midwestern, Eastern and Southeastern states. Hoven said Revco has no outlets in Alabama, Mississippi or the Florida panhandle.
Hoven said Revco planned to incorporate Big B's stores under the Revco banner if the tender offer proved successful.
Big B said it would "carefully consider" the unsolicited offer and asked shareholders to defer decisions on whether to tender their stock until they were advised of Big B's position.
Analysts said the move was part of a wider trend toward consolidation among drugstore chains.
"There is terrific pressure in the industry for consolidation and for smaller, regional players and independents to say bye-bye and join bigger chains," said Salomon Brothers's Jonathan Ziegler.
On Monday, Big B Inc shares closed up 3-1/4 at 15-7/8 on the Nasdaq. Revco finished on the New York Stock Exchange down 1/8 to 25-1/2.
Giblen said the dip in Revco's price was likely because investors recalled Revco's initial difficulties in absorbing Hook, which in the long term was "an excellent acquisition."
To be sure, Revco could experience "acquisition indigestion" with Big B, he said. The Alabama-based chain earned $0.15 a share in the year ended February 3 versus $0.97 a share the previous year.

Chriss Street of Chriss Street & Co said Revco was "the natural buyer" for Big B because Revco's advanced technology and inventory management systems enable it to improve profit margins at retail drugstores in a managed-care environment.

Revco, which began buying Big B stock in mid-August, owns about 5.4 percent of Big B's fully diluted 22 million common shares, Hoven said. The tender offer for all outstanding shares is valued at about $330 million (fully diluted).
Revco launched the offer after it was rebuffed by Big B. Hoven said Revco was willing to structure a stock deal.
But, he warned, "if the Big B board takes any action to block our offer, we're committed to this transaction and will take whatever action seems appropriate at the time" to complete it.
